items.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
items.blurb: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself.

items.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
items.blurb: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation?

items.title: Ancestral and derived feeding morphology during rapid ecological divergence within a species
items.blurb: Derived characters that may have emerged via positive selection can be identified by comparing species, but also possibly subgroups within species. Allopatric and sympatric polymorphism observed in many salmonids is thought to emerge mainly in landlocked populations, which have lost the anadromous lifestyle of their ancestors. Populations of Arctic charr (Salvelinus alpinus) are an example of such polymorphism, commonly diverging along a pelagic-benthic axis. Populations of Icelandic charr can be anadromous or landlocked, like in Lake Thingvallavatn where four morphs coexist differing in habitat use, preferred prey and external feeding morphology. Three of these morphs are also caught in the neighboring Lake Ulfljotsvatn, despite prey availability in the two lakes differing notably. We studied variation of craniofacial morphology in Icelandic charr populations and compared the ecologically specialized sympatric morphs to five anadromous charr populations and to two non-specialized lake populations, as well as across two connected lakes. The results indicate minor variation among anadromous populations and that the benthic lake forms are derived. There was clear phenotypic difference between benthic and pelagic morphs within Thingvallavatn but no differences between the morphs in Ulfljotsvatn. Patterns of variation between corresponding morphs across the two lakes suggest genetics separation and phenotypic plasticity.

items.title: Differential population declines across migratory strategies are shifting European bird communities towards residency
items.blurb: Previous studies revealed steep declines in populations of common migratory birds across Europe, especially for long-distance migrants. However, these studies focussed on continental-scale patterns, and they assigned a single migratory strategy to each species, often not distinguishing short-distance migrants from residents. It thus remains unclear whether the same patterns are found across European countries, and whether they hold when taking into account the variation in migratory behaviour observed across the European populations of many species. Here, we examine how European breeding landbird communities have varied according to migratory strategy between 1990 and 2023, at both continental and national scales. By compiling multiple sources of information on seasonal movements, we characterise the migratory strategy of landbird populations per country (long-distance migrant, short-distance migrant or resident). We combined these data with estimates of population trends and of abundance from national monitoring schemes to quantify changes in both multi-species indices (average change across species) and total abundance of birds, for each migratory strategy. At the continental scale, multi-species indices reveal a strong decline in long-distance migrants (-26.8% between 1990 and 2023), whereas short-distance migrants declined more slowly (-4.5%) and residents remained stable. Changes in total abundance show even steeper declines - of 29.9% and 10.2% for, respectively, long- and short-distance migrants - whereas residents increased slightly (+3.4%). Together, these results point to a gradual reorganisation of bird communities towards a greater dominance of resident birds across Europe. However, these changes are not happening homogenously across the continent: whereas in Central and Southern Europe we observed the same general pattern of declining migrants while residents remained broadly stable or increased, in Northern Europe we reveal declines for all migratory strategies. Overall, our study highlights the widespread vulnerability of migratory birds in Europe, while showing that the reorganisation of bird communities follows different trajectories across regions.

items.title: Normalised whole-plant water supply declines with plant height across the seed-plant phylogeny
items.blurb: Whole-plant water-transport capacity largely controls terrestrial water fluxes, yet it is unresolved to what extent its variation across the seed-plant phylogeny is structured by shared ancestry, edaphoclimatic conditions, plant height or water relation traits. We fitted a phylogenetic structural equation model to maximum leaf-specific whole-plant hydraulic conductance (kL), together with concurrent Huber value (Hv), stomatal conductance (gs), and height for 263 species spanning the global climate space, partitioning direct from indirect effects, and phylogenetically conserved from independent effects. kL declined with height, and Hv did not offset this decline. Hv raised kL but was unrelated to height among species. kL was lower in wetter niches, despite higher Hv there, indicating lower conductance per unit sapwood area. kL was tightly coupled to gs in both conserved and independent variation, so the height-driven decline in kL propagated to gas exchange. Plant height therefore constrains whole-plant hydraulic supply and, through it, gs.

items.title: Monolayer, Spheroid, and Organoid Formats Elicit Proteomic States that Couple Organelle Organization to Metabolic Vulnerabilities
items.blurb: Three-dimensional (3D) cell culture systems are becoming more widely applied to model tissue organization, disease progression, and therapeutic response. Yet, the molecular characteristics that distinguish organoids and spheroids from conventional monolayer culture are incompletely defined. Here, using tumorigenic organoid models of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian cancer (HGSC), we establish a quantitative proteomic resource that reveals how cell architecture and media independently but jointly shape the cellular state in organoids, spheroids, and monolayers. We further pursue HGSC subtype-enriched features within this framework and identify that a poor prognosis-associated genotype with reported paclitaxel hypersensitivity, Trp53-/-;Pten-/-;Nf1-/- (PPN), is marked by increased microtubule-associated proteins, lipid-associated factors, and mitochondrial remodeling. PPN cells displayed clustered lipid droplets, whereby mitochondria-ER tethering increased. Relative to Trp53-/- (P) and a frequent HGSC genotype, Trp53-/-;Brca1+/-;MycOE (PBM), live-cell imaging showed that PPN exhibits the highest degree of stable mitochondria-ER encapsulations, coincident with fission-biased mitochondria and a high-flux respiratory state. Disruption of the mitochondria-ER contact protein PTPIP51 reduced lipid droplet clustering in the PPN state. Because cytomegalovirus is known to exploit host mitochondria remodeling, mitochondria-ER contacts, and metabolic output during infection, we tested whether this pre-existing host configuration is associated with cytomegalovirus permissiveness. PPN organoids exhibited greater murine cytomegalovirus infection and infectious output than matched monolayers or PBM. Together, these data define a resource of distinct protein characteristics between matched monolayer, spheroid, and organoid systems that should be considered for experimental design. We also uncover a mechanistic axis connecting 3D architecture, organelle contacts, metabolism, drug response, and viral permissiveness.

items.title: A multi-scale forecasting framework to prioritize clinically-relevant antibiotic resistance alleles
items.blurb: Established in vitro measures for the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, a critical global threat, can fail to predict which in vitro discovered mutations will dominate in the real world following widespread antibiotic use. Here, we introduce a multi-scale computational framework integrating genetic constraints and population pharmacokinetics and apply it to explain resistance allele success in Acinetobacter baumannii for the historic case of resistance to the fluoroquinolone antibiotic ciprofloxacin. By coupling intrinsic nucleotide substitution likelihoods with continuous-time stochastic modeling under fluctuating drug exposures, our framework clearly prioritizes the most common real world gyrA fluoroquinolone resistance allele S81L over rarer alleles, reflecting its clinical success. While gyrA serves as a proof-of-concept case study for direct, active-site drug-target interactions where the target space is constrained, we observe that the nucleotide substitution likelihoods are not explaining allele success in resistance-determining genes pmrB and adeS. Furthermore, "virtual twin" cohort simulations reveal that restricted drug penetration or compromised immunity expands selective windows, rescuing rare, low-fitness alleles. This advances our understanding of prospective, model-informed risk prediction during antibiotic development.

items.title: Klebsiella taiwanensis sp. nov., and Pseudomonas ficus sp. nov., novel taxa isolated from figs (Ficus)
items.blurb: Two bacterial strains, WOUb02T and WOUb67T, were isolated from fresh figs (Ficus spp.) collected from the island of Taiwan. Cells of WOUb02T and WOUb67T were Gram-stain-negative rods. Strain WOUb02T was non-motile, whereas WOUb67T exhibited motility. Physiologically, both strains grew optimally at 0.5% (w/v) NaCl and pH 8.0; WOUb02T grew optimally at 37{degrees}C, whereas WOUb67T grew optimally at 30{degrees}C. Based on 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity, the closest relatives to strains WOUb02T and WOUb67T were Klebsiella terrigena ATCC 33257T (98.2%) and Pseudomonas putida NBRC 14164T (99.9%) respectively. Subsequent phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that strains WOUb02T and WOUb67T formed distinct lineages within the genera Klebsiella and Pseudomonas, respectively. Further genomic analyses revealed that WOUb02T and WOUb67T shared average nucleotide identity and digital DNA-DNA hybridization values <95.0% and <70.0%, below the currently accepted thresholds for species-level delineation. Based on phenotypic and genotypic data, strains WOUb02T and WOUb67T could be distinguished from other species with validly published names and are considered to represent novel species in the genera Klebsiella and Pseudomonas, respectively, for which the names Klebsiella taiwanensis sp. nov., and Pseudomonas ficus sp. nov., are proposed. The type strains are WOUb02T (=NRRL-B 65719T =CCUG 77855T) and WOUb67T (=NRRL-B 65720T =CCUG 77856T).

items.title: Effect of Moisture Content of Paddy (Phka Rumduol) on the Quality of White Rice (Oryza sativa L.)
items.blurb: This study evaluated the impact of paddy moisture content on the quality parameters of white rice produced from Cambodia's premium fragrant variety, Phka Rumduol (Oryza sativa L.). A completely randomized design (CRD) was employed to evaluate the effect of moisture content on rice quality. Paddy samples were adjusted to four target moisture levels (10%, 12%, 14%, and 16%) and subsequently milled under controlled conditions. The CRD ensured unbiased allocation of samples across all treatments, minimizing experimental error during both moisture conditioning and milling processes. The results showed that moisture content had a significant effect (p < 0.05) on all measured quality parameters. Paddy at 14% moisture content produced the best results, with a head rice yield of 63.46 %, and a broken rice percentage of only 4.86 %. Grain appearance was also well preserved, with rice bran yield of 10.67 %, rice husk yield of 18.52 %, and yellow kernels averaging just 0.79 %. In contrast, moisture levels below 12% increased kernel brittleness, leading to breakage rates as high as 26.28 %, while levels above 16% caused grain deformation and discoloration. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining paddy moisture at 14% prior to milling to optimize recovery and preserve the high quality of Phka Rumduol rice. The study provides practical guidance for Cambodian rice processors aiming to improve product quality and strengthen competitiveness in international markets.

items.title: Molecular dynamics simulations and in vivo binding studies indicate distinct membrane binding modes of plant lipid droplet proteins including binding via a hydrophobic face
items.blurb: Plant lipid droplets (LDs) are specialized cellular subcompartments for lipid storage and key hubs for lipid metabolism. They have a unique structure: a hydrophobic core composed of neutral lipids enclosed by a phospholipid monolayer and associated proteins. Progress has been made in the identification and characterization of LD-associated plant proteins in recent years, raising the question of how these proteins bind to LDs. To investigate common structural features of LD association, we set up an in silico system using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the nature of this interaction and to identify predicted binding regions of selected proteins. We then tested the importance of these regions for LD association by transient expression of truncated or mutated variants in tobacco pollen tubes. With this combined approach, we investigated the LD targeting region of thirteen LD-associated proteins. In several proteins, a distinct structural feature, a hydrophobic face, binds to LDs by interacting with the acyl chains of the phospholipid monolayer through large hydrophobic residues thereby pushing the headgroups to the sides. We also analyzed proteins previously assayed for LD association and demonstrate a correlation between predicted binding parameters and in vivo binding.

items.title: Mitochondrial H2S and cytochrome c coordinate guard cell redox dynamics during stomatal immunity
items.blurb: Stomatal pores modulate gas exchange between plants and the environment and are the first layer of defense against pathogens entry. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is a recognized component of the signalling network in guard cells that control stomatal responses. We previously showed that the mitochondrial H2S source {beta}-cyanoalanine synthase (CAS-C1) is required for flg22-induced stomatal closure. Using genetically encoded redox biosensors in Arabidopsis thaliana guard cells, we found that the mitochondrially-targeted H2S donor AP39 and the pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) flg22 both increased mitochondrial H2O2 within 5 min, while the flg22-triggered rise was attenuated in cas-c1 mutants. Dissipating the mitochondrial membrane potential ({Delta}{psi}m) with the uncoupler 2,4-dinitrophenol prevented both mitochondrial oxidation and stomatal closure. Cytochrome c (CYTc), the mobile electron carrier between complexes III and IV, proved essential for this pathway. CYTc-deficient lines showed a stomatal response similar than wild-type (wt) to ABA and light but failed to trigger stomatal closure upon exposure to different PAMPs. In these plants, neither AP39 nor flg22 induced guard cell mitochondrial hyperpolarization or an increase in cytosolic H2O2. By the dimedone-switch method, we show that CYTc is persulfidated in vivo, identifying this respiratory protein as a target of H2S-mediated posttranslational modification. At the whole-plant level, cytc plants were more susceptible to spray inoculation with Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato hrcC- at early stages of infection. Together, these results position CYTc as a mitochondrial node that links H2S signalling to guard cell redox dynamics during stomatal immunity.

items.blurb:
The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books

I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation.

We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.”

items.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis? | Bill McGuire
items.blurb:
Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like

It’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature record could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region.

We continue to pump out the CO2 weight-equivalent of 800,000 Titanics every year, with no end in sight. Meanwhile the latest climate Cop – the only global initiative with the potential to turn things around – has just collapsed in disarray, unable to get its act together even to agree on a vague form of words about the need to transition away from fossil fuels.

items.blurb:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

  • Republican senators criticize Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang


The surge in stock markets since Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced shows that investors are “willing to re-engage with the AI theme when uncertainty recedes”, says Christian Stocker, lead equity strategist for UniCredit Munich.

But… Stocker argues that the rally reflected relief that the AI supply chain and investment cycle are unlikely to be abruptly disrupted, rather than renewed conviction that all concerns have disappeared.

Questions about financing structures, profitability and the ultimate returns on AI spending remain largely unresolved.

In other words, the debate has shifted. Investors are no longer asking whether AI investment will continue. They are increasingly asking whether the path from investment to monetisation will be slower, more uneven and more dependent on favourable financing conditions than previously assumed. Recent market volatility suggests that the AI narrative remains intact, but the market is becoming less willing to assume a straight-line path to future earnings growth.

With fears of an AI slowdown receding, it also led markets to price back in a more hawkish path for the Federal Reserve over the months ahead.

So for the next meeting in December, markets are once again fully pricing in a 25bp hike, with 26.1bps priced in for that decision (+3.1bps on the day). Then looking further out, 70bps of hikes are now priced in by the September 2027 meeting, up +6.6bps relative to Friday

items.title: Ukraine: Returns to unsafe frontline areas: drivers of return and intentions to stay in Khersonska, Zaporizka and Sumska Oblasts, November 2026 [EN/UK]
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached files.

Introduction

Between June and July 2026, REACH in partnership with local NGOs Unity and Strength and Tenth of April conducted three assessments on unsafe returns (returns within 30 kilometres of the front line and/or the border with the Russian Federation) in Khersonska, Sumska and Zaporizka Oblasts. Interviewing 89 returnees with diverse displacement experiences (e.g., displaced abroad, displaced within the oblast), vulnerabilities (e.g., spent savings) and factors of resilience (e.g., owned housing), REACH examined what drove returnees away from “safer” locations, what pulled them to areas with ongoing insecurity, and their needs post-return.

Returns to unsafe areas remain a persistent concern for the humanitarian response in Ukraine. An estimated 4.2 million people had returned to their areas of origin or habitual residence as of May 2026. Returns to areas within 30 kilometres of the front line or the border accounted for roughly one-third of IDP returns since February 2022, an estimated 1.6 million people. The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan identifies returns to unsafe areas both as a protection risk and as a negative coping mechanism among people in prolonged displacement. The assessments aim to inform programming that 1) meets returnees’ specific needs in unsafe areas, and 2) improves conditions in areas of displacement to avoid returns made out of pressure rather than choice.

Across Khersonska, Sumska and Zaporizka Oblasts, respondents returned to frontline areas despite the (increased) insecurity – the initial trigger of their displacement. Most had left because of occupation, shelling or a specific attack; these threats remained at the time of interview, and respondents were aware of them when deciding to return. Some described insecurity in locations of displacement, such as Kyiv and Odesa, as equivalent to the security considerations that had triggered their displacement, while others felt the pressures (e.g., family separation) and vulnerabilities (e.g., spent savings) accrued in displacement eventually outweighed security conditions.

Economic pressure and relational and emotional factors appeared as key considerations in all three assessments. Return mostly followed a period in which displacement became difficult to sustain – due to rent, depleted savings, social isolation or family separation – rather than an improvement in security at home. These accounts indicate that negative experiences during displacement contributed to some respondents’ decisions to return despite continuing insecurity. Combined with ccess to owned housing, family, work or familiar services at home, respondents felt compelled to return despite the insecurity. Return reduced some pressures but did not resolve all needs. Some returnees struggled to recover from displacement even after return, for example due to accumulated home repairs or debt. As return at times prolonged or exacerbated vulnerabilities (rather than addressing them), continued insecurity may displace returnees again. Respondents’ intentions to stay were often conditional on security, housing and services. Households facing repeated displacement may be particularly vulnerable, as repeated moves are likely to erode coping capacities over time.

Differences in return decisions and post-return experiences were clearer between groups of respondents than between oblasts. Those who were older, displaced for shorter periods, displaced from occupied territories or displaced abroad were often flagged as particularly vulnerable post-return, while returnees to rural areas often had diverging experiences from those returning to urban areas.

This summary presents the key findings of REACH’s Unsafe Returns assessments. Oblastspecific information can be found in the Khersonska, Sumska and Zaporizka briefs.

items.title: Haiti: Haïti | Initiative Conjointe de Suivi des Marchés (ICSM) : Panier de Dépenses Minimales (MEB) Non Alimentaire et Estimation de la Valeur de Transfert (10 - 15 août 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Haiti
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached file.

RÉSULTATS CLÉS

• Lors du cycle d’août 2026, le coût du MEB multisectoriel non alimentaire était le plus élevé dans la ZMPAP, aussi bien pour le panier de crise prolongée que pour celui d’urgence. À l’inverse, le Nord-Est enregistrait les coûts les plus faibles pour les deux paniers. Ces disparités pourraient notamment refléter des différences dans les conditions d’approvisionnement et les coûts de transport.

• Aucun des 23 marchés évalués ne présente une fonctionnalité complète ou limitée : 15 présentent des problèmes sévères et 8 une fonctionnalité pauvre. Les principales faiblesses concernent l’abordabilité, la résilience des approvisionnements et les infrastructures, tandis que l’accessibilité physique et la disponibilité des produits obtiennent des résultats relativement plus favorables.

• Les difficultés d’approvisionnement varient selon les marchés évalués. Si 23% des vendeurs interrogés rapportent au moins une rupture de stock au cours du mois précédant l’enquête, cette proportion atteint 46% dans la ZMPAP et le NordOuest. Par ailleurs, les prix élevés des fournisseurs (41%) et le manque de fonds (33%) constituent les principales contraintes rapportées par les vendeurs pour maintenir leur approvisionnement.

items.title: Syria: Humanitarian Situation Monitoring (HSM), November 2026 [EN/AR]
items.blurb:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached files.

KEY MESSAGES

• Livelihoods (68%) and food (66%) emerged as the two leading priority needs reported by KIs in assessed communities, largely driven by rising living costs. Nearly two-thirds of KIs (65%) reported substantial increases in living costs, while 94% of those reporting food-related difficulties cited the inability to afford food or associated fuel and transportation costs.

• Winterisation was the third most frequently reported priority need (53%), with rising heating fuel costs and inadequate electricity availability compounding seasonal vulnerabilities and increasing the risk that households will be forced to divert limited resources from food and other essential needs to maintain adequate warmth during winter.

• Rising fuel prices acted as a multi-sectoral crisis multiplier, driving up the costs of food, transportation, heating, agricultural production and essential services, with 92% of KIs identifying fuel price increases as a key driver of rising household costs.

• Deir-ez-Zor, Al-Hasakeh and Dar’a emerged as key areas of concern. In Deir-ez-Zor, livelihood deterioration and winterisation needs overlapped with food unaffordability and WASH and healthcare gaps; in Al-Hasakeh, severe food insecurity, winterisation pressures and limited access to essential services were compounded by declining purchasing power; while Dar’a faced overlapping water, shelter, livelihood and healthcare challenges.

items.title: Syria: Fuel Price Increases - Emerging Impacts and Outlook (November 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: REACH Initiative

Please refer to the attached file.

KEY MESSAGES

• Fuel price increases are reaching households mainly through higher transport and heating costs. Effects on other prices are so far limited: water trucking prices may be starting to rise, while food prices have remained relatively stable, indicating a need for close price monitoring.

• Rising transport costs are restricting households’ access to markets where essentials remain available. Increasing transport costs could particularly hit Al-Hasakeh and Ar-Raqqa, where around 40% of KIs reported that households rely on markets outside their community. Multi-purpose cash remains appropriate, except where markets may be facing shortages, such as fuel and core goods in As-Sweida.

• Fuel price increases are likely to further erode households’ living conditions as winter starts. Nearly half of KIs (47%) reported that households relied on purchased energy for heating. At October prices, the same amount of money buys about 30% less diesel than in August.

• In Al-Hasakeh and Deir-ez-Zor, fuel-dependent heating and water services coexist with widespread winter needs. As-Sweida faces the most acute price and supply pressures

items.title: Briefing by Alexander De Croo, UNDP Administrator, to the UN Security Council on energy, needs and reconstruction efforts in Ukraine
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN Development Programme

As prepared for delivery

Mr. President, Members of the Security Council,

1. [Introduction]

Three hundred and seventy-two civilians killed.
Nearly two thousand injured.
Last month was the deadliest October since the full-scale invasion began.

And as winter approaches, the suffering is deepening.

Across Ukraine, repeated attacks are depriving civilians of heat, electricity, water and healthcare, services they need to survive.

Today, the front line extends far beyond the battlefield.

It runs through homes, hospitals, schools and businesses, and through the daily lives of millions of Ukrainians, victims of a war that is not of their own making.

The unprecedented scale with which Ukrainian energy and water grids have been attacked, can no longer be considered collateral damage. It is deliberately making life for ordinary citizens nearly impossible.

Air-raid sirens can sound at any hour.

Power cuts force hospitals to postpone procedures, schools to close and businesses to suspend operations. Disruptions to water and sanitation increase the risk to public health.

When I visited Ukraine in September, I saw this reality first-hand. I met people restoring essential services and rebuilding their communities while the war continued around them.

As one local partner told me: “We are not rebuilding after the war. We are rebuilding during the war.”

[Attacks on energy infrastructure and their impact on civilians]

Mr. President,

Last winter showed the scale of that challenge.

Ukraine’s energy infrastructure suffered damage on an unprecedented scale, leaving a gap of six gigawatts in generation capacity.

Extensive repairs helped stabilize the system over the summer.

But since mid-July, attacks have intensified. In some cases, energy facilities have been struck again before repair crews could finish their work.

Since October, attacks have increasingly targeted the high-voltage substations and transmission lines supplying major cities.

On 12 November alone, nearly 700,000 families were reportedly left without electricity.

For many Ukrainians, electricity can no longer be taken for granted.

People no longer count the hours without power. They count the precious hours when they have it.

This is far more than an infrastructure challenge.

It is a humanitarian challenge.
A development challenge.
And it is a direct threat to civilian resilience.

2. [UNDP’s support for emergency energy restoration and recovery]

UNDP is working with Ukraine’s national and local authorities to restore power today while supporting longer-term recovery.

This goes to the heart of our development mandate: keeping essential services running, protecting livelihoods and helping communities function.

We have supplied transformers to help restore the grid, and delivered generators and power stations to provide power locally.

Our energy support has reached 435 communities across all 24 regions. An estimated 6.7 million people benefit from improvements to energy, heating and water infrastructure.

In September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Energy and UNDP launched the Ukraine Energy Installation Facility to bring urgently needed energy equipment into service faster.

Our emergency energy support covers the full cycle, from design to installation and commissioning.

But repairing what was damaged is not enough. We are also helping Ukraine build a cleaner, more decentralized and resilient energy system through greater energy efficiency and passive protection for critical infrastructure.

Our objective is to restore the power and heat people need to survive this winter, while strengthening the energy system for the years ahead.

3. [Mine action]

Mr. President,

Mine action is fundamental to recovery.

Until land is safe, fields cannot be farmed, families cannot return home and communities cannot be rebuilt.

As we have heard from the World Food Programme, Ukraine’s ability to grow and ship food matters far beyond its borders. But food production begins with safe land.

UNDP supports the Government in surveying contaminated areas and prioritizing clearance.

To date, some 42,000 square kilometres of land have been returned to productive use.

4. [UNDP’s support for Ukraine’s wider recovery]

In war-damaged communities, making the land safe is only the beginning.

Debris must be cleared. Homes, schools and hospitals must be rebuilt. Public services must be restored. And people need livelihoods that allow them to return and rebuild their lives.

That is why UNDP works across the full recovery chain, from making communities safe to restoring the foundations of daily life.

With around 500 personnel working in Kyiv and six regional hubs, we support communities, including in front-line areas.

We help local authorities plan their recovery, repair homes and public buildings, equip health facilities and refurbish air-raid shelters, including in schools.

We help local businesses reopen, support young people and families returning home.

And make it easier for people to access public services online and through mobile teams.

Recovery must reach those who carry the scars of the battlefield.

That means helping veterans return to civilian life and supporting their families through that transition.

Local veterans’ centres bring rehabilitation, psychological support, legal advice, and training and employment services together under one roof.

Across, 13 oblasts, more than 1.3 million people benefit from UNDP-supported (local) recovery programmes.

Recovery also requires investment at scale.

UNDP’s technical assistance has also helped Ukraine unlock nearly US$1.6 billion in European Investment Bank financing to rebuild schools, hospitals and other essential infrastructure.

None of this would be possible without our donors. Their support keeps essential services running, helps communities rebuild and gives families hope for the future.

[Conclusion]

Mr. President, distinguished members of the Council,

Our responsibility is not only to help Ukrainians endure another winter.

It is to ensure that the support provided today lays the foundations for recovery tomorrow.

That is what development from day one means.

Ukraine is leading this effort, and UNDP is there to support it.

The people I met appreciate the UN presence and the work we are doing, but what they really need, is for this war to end.

And for this they look to you, Members of this Council, to help deliver it.

Thank you.

items.title: Ethiopia: Lethal artillery strikes on civilian neighbourhoods in Tigray’s Alamata city must be investigated as war crimes
items.blurb:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: Amnesty International

Please refer to the attached file.

Artillery attacks by Ethiopia’s military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm’s way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.

The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.

“For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants. The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes,” said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International’s Senior Director, Regional Human Rights Impact.

“For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants.

Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for Human Rights Impact

Amnesty International investigated four incidents of artillery shelling on Alamata by the ENDF and TPF between 26 and 28 September and independently verified the deaths of 14 civilians in these attacks. Researchers interviewed 28 individuals, including survivors, witnesses, relatives of victims, humanitarian and medical personnel. Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab analysed eight videos and 17 photographs, as well as satellite imagery of the site and other open-source information.

All names and identifying details have been withheld or changed to protect interviewees who requested anonymity.

Amnesty International wrote to the ENDF, TPF, and TPLF on 27 October, requesting information about these incidents. On 17 November, the organization shared its investigation findings with the ENDF and TPF and invited their comments. ENDF and TPF had not provided a response as at the time of publication.

The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes.

Yasmine Ahmed

In a four-page letter sent to Amnesty International on 18 November, the TPLF “categorically reject[ed]’’ the allegations made against it.

“While the preliminary findings acknowledge certain atrocities committed by the Ethiopian Federal Government and its forces we are deeply concerned by the allegations directed against the Tigray Security Forces [TPLF]. We categorically reject these allegations as unfounded and believe that they require further independent, impartial, and comprehensive investigation before any conclusions are drawn regarding responsibility’’ stated the letter sent by the TPLF.

Residential neighbourhoods at the mercy of ENDF and TPF Artillery shelling

Based on interviews with residents and two sources with direct knowledge of military movements during the offensive, Amnesty International identified Waja Ena Tumuga area as the main location from which ENDF and TPF forces shelled Alamata, approximately 13 kilometers south of the city. Two individuals with close knowledge of the TPF’s military capabilities told the organization that the TPF possessed artillery weaponry and participated alongside the ENDF in the operation to capture Alamata. One eyewitness saw ENDF forces moving their artillery into Waja, particularly the area that is called Ayer Marefiya.

Witnesses also told Amnesty International that the TPLF based themselves in and, in some instances, launched attacks from densely populated civilian areas in the city.

International humanitarian law requires all parties to a conflict to avoid, to the maximum extent feasible, placing military objectives within or near densely populated areas. They are also obliged to protect civilians from the effects of attacks by facilitating the evacuation of civilians from the vicinity of military objectives and giving effective warning of attacks that may affect the civilian population.

Any possible violation of international humanitarian law by TPLF through placing their forces and military objects inside densely populated neighbourhoods, does not absolve the ENDF and its allies of their obligations and can never justify the indiscriminate use of explosive weapons, such as artillery, in a densely populated area.

Yasmine Ahmed

Even though TPLF fighters possessed artillery capabilities and were actively launching artillery, it is highly unlikely that the shelling of Alamata was caused by direct shelling from their own forces within the city. While the possibility of technical failures cannot be fully dismissed, the likelihood of such a scenario is extremely low.

“Any possible violation of international humanitarian law by TPLF through placing their forces and military objects inside densely populated neighbourhoods, does not absolve the ENDF and its allies of their obligations and can never justify the indiscriminate use of explosive weapons, such as artillery, in a densely populated area,” said Yasmine Ahmed.

A medical worker, who was on duty in Alamata hospital between 26 and 28 September, told Amnesty International that almost all casualties recorded during those three days were civilians and that most of the injuries appeared to have been caused by shrapnel from explosive munitions.

Indiscriminate attacks on populated areas

One of the neighbourhoods most heavily hit by shelling was an area commonly known as the condominium area in Kebele 04, a densely populated area comprised mostly of houses and two multi-story buildings, which house hundreds of civilians and are adjacent to the single-family homes that were struck. Three eyewitnesses told Amnesty International that artillery struck five houses on 27 September at dawn, killing seven people and injuring four others.

Among those killed was Meron Sewasew, a 26-year-old mother of two, who died inside her home alongside her eight-year-old son, Markon Girmahiwot, and her older brother, Tewekel Sewasew, 33. Meron’s husband, Girmahiwot Negash [real name], said their two-year-old son was also in the house at the time of the attack but survived with minor injuries.

“I was away from the city for work. They were staying in the house because it was supposed to be safe from the war. She was my high school love, and our story ended too soon,” Girmahiwot said.

The same artillery attack also killed four members of a family living next door: Kumhis Kahsay, 40, and her 14-year-old child Helina Hailay, alongside Lezeu Yirga, 38, and her three-year old child.

I was away from the city for work. They were staying in the house because it was supposed to be safe from the war. She was my high school love, and our story ended too soon.

Girmahiwot

“Kumhis came from church that morning. All of the victims were outside the house doing chores. Kumhis, the older sister, was baking injera in the compound. I was inside the house. The remnants of the strike landed in the compound and struck them,” said a family member who survived the attack.

Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab verified four videos that showed damage to the two houses and one external structure within a compound located some 150 meters from Werknesh Hotel, a hotel which residents said had housed TPLF fighters.

“I saw TDF [TPLF] fighters on top of tall buildings with their weapons. They were telling us not to come closer. Some were staying at the Werknesh Hotel…. they were telling people to use a different route,” said an eyewitness who was in the area on 26 September.

Another individual who was near the hotel on the day of the attack told Amnesty International that TPLF fighters were not present near the hotel on the day of the strike. Amnesty International could not independently verify whether TPLF fighters were inside or near the hotel at the time. Three eyewitnesses said that minutes before artillery shells struck nearby residential homes, a separate strike fell just outside the hotel, causing significant damage to its exterior.

The ENDF and TPF also shelled areas where residents said there was no military presence.

On 26 September, artillery hit a local bar called Nigus Shimoy at around 11am, killing at least three people, according to a survivor who was injured in the attack and one witness. The bar is located at the entrance of a bustling market in a predominantly commercial area, bordering residential neighbourhoods. The attack took place as people came out en masse to celebrate Demera, the eve celebration of Meskel (Finding of the True Cross) holiday of the Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

I saw TDF [TPLF] fighters on top of tall buildings with their weapons. They were telling us not to come closer. Some were staying at the Werknesh Hotel…. they were telling people to use a different route.

Eyewitness

On 27 September, shelling hit a family home in another residential area, Kebele 02. Deyima Rebso, 55, was killed immediately in the attack in her home, while her husband, Ararse Yasin, 62, survived with severe injuries, according to an eyewitness. Their children, Saliha and Kedir, and grandchild, 10-year-old Sufiyan Abdulatif, also sustained serious injuries. Amnesty International’s weapons investigator identified munitions fragments recovered at the scene as consistent with an artillery round of the type fired by the ENDF and their allies.

One witness told Amnesty International that the house was the only structure to be struck in the area and that no military activity had been observed in the vicinity prior to the attack.

TPLF set up military bases in schools

Six people interviewed by Amnesty International said almost all schools in Alamata were used by TPLF fighters as military bases in the months before the outbreak of renewed hostilities. Witnesses said several schools, most of which were located close to civilian neighbourhoods, had been the site of military operations, including the launching of artillery shells after the renewed conflict began. All residents interviewed for this research said the TPLF didn’t issue any warnings or evacuation orders for residents near these locations.

On 26 September, an artillery shell struck a house in a highly populated neighbourhood known as Missionary Camp, near to Biruh Tesfa School, which had been used by the TPLF as a base. The attack, which occurred at around 6:45 pm, killed three civilians and injured four others. One witness said most of the fighters had left a week before the fighting broke out. Another saw a few fighters guarding the school in the days leading up to the strike.

Amnesty International could not independently confirm whether the school was ever attacked and whether or not the school was still harbouring fighters by the time of the strike. No damage or destruction was clearly visible in satellite imagery at the Biruh Tesfa school north of the charity compound.

A resident living near Alamata Preparatory School, another school, said that the school was targeted by an ENDF drone strike on 22 September. He said the school had been the main site from which TPLF launched artillery strikes to defend Alamata, until they began withdrawing from the city on 28 September.

“The explosion of weapons after it was hit by drone strikes affected the city, and we also saw some remnants fly by my house. There was artillery inside the school compound. We saw the weapons burning in the school that day,” said the resident.

Satellite imagery confirms a new burn scar became visible adjacent to the school on 22 September, aligning with the reports of a drone strike. Changes in vegetation were also detected around the school between 24 September and 1 October, though high-resolution imagery is not available to confirm the reason for the changes. Higher-resolution imagery from 21 October shows the clearing in more detail, along with a burned area within the trees.

False-colour, near infrared satellite imagery shows the preparatory school, highlighted with a white box. Healthy vegetation appears in red hues while recently burned areas appear black. On 19 September 2026, satellite imagery shows the vegetation surrounding the school appears healthy. On 23 September 2026, imagery shows a dark area within the vegetation – highlighted in yellow, suggesting the area was recently burned. Higher resolution imagery from 21 October 2026 confirms the area within the yellow circle appears burned

“Civilians are paying the ultimate price for the failure to hold perpetrators accountable in past and ongoing conflicts in Ethiopia. Impunity has emboldened perpetrators to carry on committing serious violations with no fear of the consequences. This must end. The UN Human Rights Council must act fast to establish an independent mechanism to investigate, identify those responsible for crimes under international law, and ensure they are held accountable,” said Yasmine Ahmed.

“Amnesty International also calls on the Ethiopian authorities to cooperate with independent international monitors, journalists, and humanitarian organizations to gain unhindered access to all conflict-impacted areas in the country.

Impunity has emboldened perpetrators to carry on committing serious violations with no fear of the consequences. This must end. The UN Human Rights Council must act fast to establish an independent mechanism to investigate, identify those responsible for crimes under international law, and ensure they are held accountable.

Yasmine Ahmed

“Considering the Ethiopian authorities’ persistent failure to ensure justice and accountability for crimes under international law, particularly where state forces themselves are alleged to have committed serious violations, urgent international scrutiny is needed. This is especially critical given the authorities’ record of suppressing independent human rights monitoring and the fact that Ethiopia is currently facing three ongoing armed conflicts, with growing risks of wider regional escalation’’ said Yasmine Ahmed.

Background

The armed conflict between the ENDF and its allies, including the TPF and other allied security and informal militia forces, and the TPLF and allies, including Amhara Fano forces and six other organized political and armed groups, erupted on 21 September 2026.

Fighting spread across three principal fronts initially: in southern Tigray, particularly the Raya Kobo Zone; western Afar (Zone 2); and the Wag Hemra Zone of the Amhara Region.

Since 21 September, the ENDF has carried out multiple aerial strikes in the southern Tigray, including in and around Alamata city.

We acknowledge the judgment of the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (Genocide Convention).

This marks an important step toward accountability and justice for Rohingya victims and survivors, and for all those affected by the ongoing atrocities being committed in Myanmar.

items.title: Syria Polio Outbreak Response | Situation Report No. 1, 22 November 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: Syrian Arab Republic, Iraq
Sources: Government of the Syrian Arab Republic, UN Children's Fund, World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

In October 2026, after receiving initial reports of children with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) in Deir ez-Zor Governorate, Syria, the Ministry of Health (MoH) mounted a swift response, in coordination with partners.

Conflict, displacement, interrupted immunization and population movement have created immunity gaps. An unrelated variant VDPV1 detection was reported in wastewater in the area in February 2026.

HIGHLIGHTS

The MoH, supported by WHO,UNICEF and partners, is leading the outbreak response, including intensified surveillance and vaccination.

Emergency vaccination activities reached:

  • 34 720 children in October 2026
  • 54 382 in November 2026 (111% of the target of 49 000)

The high coverage can be attributed to population movement. Additional efforts are needed to determine target population in future rounds.

The next campaign is planned for 30 November 2026 in six districts of Deir ez-Zor Governorate, integrating child nutrition assessments, drinking-water chlorine level checks and chlorine distribution.

An expanded scope will follow in December 2026.

The risk of further spread within Syria and to neighbouring countries, including Iraq, remains a concern due to uneven vaccination coverage and immunity gaps, particularly among displaced, mobile and underserved populations.

COORDINATION OF THE RESPONSE

The MoH is coordinating national and subnational actors. WHO and UNICEF are mobilizing regional and global technical expertise, while the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (GPEI) provides technical and financial support. World Vision and the International Rescue Committee funded the first two vaccination rounds in October and November 2026.

Two coordination meetings involving national, regional and global response teams have reviewed the situation and agreed on priorities. The MoH Incident Management Team meets weekly through its Emergency Operations Centre. The remaining 13 governorates in Syria have been advised to intensify surveillance and preparedness. Cross-border coordination is particularly important for Iraq, given population movements and the history of wild poliovirus transmission across this border in 2013.

items.title: Malawi – District Profile: Chikwawa (October 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Malawi
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

Under the Regional Response to Climate Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa (RE2CLID) program, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is implementing activities across eight districts in Malawi: Blantyre, Blantyre City, Chikwawa, Dowa, Mangochi, Mulanje, Nsanje and Phalombe. The district profiles bring together available data on population, climate hazards, displacement, vulnerability and local capacities in Chikwawa and will be complemented by the forthcoming RE2CLID Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) baseline assessment.

This profile is focused on Chikwawa District, which has experienced recurrent climate-related displacement associated with floods, tropical storms, cyclones and drought. The five Traditional Authorities (TAs) targeted by RE2CLID – Ngabu, Lundu, Makhwira, Maseya and Ngowe – were home to 348,079 people according to the 2018 Census, representing approximately 62 per cent of the district's population.

Historical DTM assessments show that these TAs also accounted for a high proportion of displacement recorded during major flood and storm events: approximately 94 per cent during the 2015 floods, 99 per cent during Cyclone Idai and 89 per cent following Cyclone Freddy. Patterns nevertheless varied between events. Displacement was concentrated particularly in TA Lundu during the 2015 floods and Cyclone Idai, while following Cyclone Freddy, DTM recorded 111,864 IDPs across 43 sites, with the largest shares located in TA Ngabu and TA Makhwira.

Looking ahead, the 2026/27 outlook points to a multi-hazard context. Under the DCCMS Strong El Niño scenario, Chikwawa is classified as extreme drought risk, while extreme-rainfall risk increases from no threat during October–December 2026 to extreme during January–March 2027. Understanding how historical displacement patterns intersect with current and projected climate risks can help inform anticipatory action, preparedness and targeted displacement monitoring.

items.title: World: Europe — Mixed Migration Flows to Europe, Quarterly Overview (July – September 2026)
items.blurb:
Countries: World, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta, Spain, Sudan
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

In late 2015, IOM launched a Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Flow Monitoring system, aiming to monitor Mixed Migration Flows to Europe by land and sea. Since then, DTM gathers, validates and disseminates information on migrants and refugees entering Europe through four main routes:

  • Eastern Mediterranean route (EMR): arrivals by sea and land to Bulgaria, Cyprus and Greece
  • Central Mediterranean route (CMR): arrivals by sea to Italy and Malta
  • Western Mediterranean route (WMR): arrivals by sea to the Peninsular Coasts of Spain, Balearic Islands, by land to the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla
  • Western African Atlantic route (WAAR): arrivals by sea to the Canary Islands of Spain

DTM also monitors data on migrants in transit through the Western Balkan route (WBR), including data from Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, and Kosovo (UNSCR 1244, 1999). These are considered separately to prevent, to the extent possible, the double counting of the same people, crossing multiple borders. Finally, DTM compiles data on migrants entering Croatia, Romania and Slovenia by land, typically after having crossed the Western Balkans or Bulgaria.

This report presents the latest available data and trends, focusing on the third quarter of 2026 and comparing it with the same period in 2025.

  • In the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), 36,097 migrants arrived in Europe via these four routes. This represents a 42 per cent increase from previous Q2 2026 and a 24 per cent decline compared with Q3 2025. The steepest year-on-year drop was on the CMR (down 59%), followed by the EMR (down 13%). Arrivals were distributed across the CMR to Italy and Malta (24%), the EMR to Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria (42%), the WMR to Spain (25%), and the WAAR to Spain (9%).
  • According to Eurostat, EU+ countries registered over 99,385 new asylum applications in the third quarter of 2026. Although data on asylum applications remain incomplete at the time of writing, France, Italy and Greece are among the highest ranking countries in the EU27+ in Q3 of 2026. Notably, France registered nearly twice as many first-time asylum applications (27,910) than Italy (15,450) did. Between July and September 2026, the main applicants held nationalities from Afghanistan (10%), Bangladesh (7%) and Sudan (6%), comprising nearly a quarter of all applications registered. These groups are followed by Türkiye, and Pakistan, Ukraine, Syrian Arab Republic and Somalia, averaging at around 4 per cent, respectively.
  • According to IOM’s MMP, 920 migrants died or went missing at sea while trying to reach Europe through the Mediterranean and Western African Atlantic routes in Q3 of 2026. Of these, 141 perished on the Central Mediterranean, and 350 while trying to cross the Atlantic to reach the Canary Islands. This represents a 6 per cent increase compared to Q3 2025 (871).

Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached files.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

October marked both one year since the October 2025 ceasefire and three years since the escalation of hostilities. The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire and extremely fragile, with humanitarian partners warning that funding shortfalls, combined with ongoing Israeli restrictions, have begun to reverse the gains achieved since the ceasefire was announced. One year on, Israeli military operations have continued and approximately 70 per cent of Gaza remains behind the constantly shifting “Yellow Line”. Most of the population remains displaced in worn-out tents, overcrowded sites and severely damaged buildings, with water and sanitation systems devastated. With the rainy season imminent, conditions are likely to worsen.

Needs ahead of winter are acute. The Shelter Cluster estimates that 1.98 million people require shelter and non-food item assistance, yet the supplies available can reach fewer than one in five of those needing shelter for winter. Winter shelter requirements remained severely underfunded, with two-thirds of the USD 283 million required still unmet. Structural safety is a growing concern, with OCHA preliminary estimates – supported by IOMled assessments – indicating that more than 4,000 buildings require full or partial demolition and some 44,000 people living in over 2,300 structurally unsafe buildings.

Briefing the Security Council on 15 October, the UN Acting Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Ramiz Alakbarov, reported that, for the fourth consecutive winter, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential equipment, spare parts, engine oil and other supplies continued to impede humanitarian and recovery efforts, and that partners knew what winter preparedness required but lacked the materials to act at the scale required. Without expanded access, the lifting of Israeli restrictions on critical materials, and adequate funding, humanitarian actors will remain unable to move from emergency relief to the recovery that Gaza urgently needs.

items.title: India Records a 38% Drop in TB Deaths: What Are Key Public Health Efforts Behind the Progress?
items.blurb: A tuberculosis diagnosis can change a person’s life. Finding the disease early, starting the right treatment and helping a patient complete it can change that course again. India’s latest figures suggest these interventions are making a measurable difference. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 estimates that India’s TB mortality rate fell from 28 deaths per lakh people in 2015 to 18 in 2025, a reduction of 38%. This is higher than the global decline of 35%. The figure reflects a public health response combining active screening, faster diagnosis, treatment and support beyond the clinic. The opportunity now is to extend these solutions and make care easier to access and complete. Finding TB before it finds the patient TB detection has often depended on people recognising symptoms and reaching a health facility. But symptoms can be overlooked or hidden by stigma. Active case-finding changes the approach: health teams take screening into communities and prioritise people at higher risk. Behind every percentage point of progress are lives saved through earlier diagnosis and sustained care. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) The TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, launched in November 2024, has expanded community-based screening. The Union Health Ministry says more than 25 crore people had been screened by November 2026, including over 11 crore chest X-rays and three crore molecular tests. The campaign reported detecting nearly 48.64 lakh cases, including almost 15 lakh people without symptoms. These are programme figures, not estimates of everyone with TB in India. Chest X-rays help identify people who need further testing, including those without obvious symptoms. Molecular tests can confirm TB and, depending on the test, identify drug resistance. WHO also records a rise in rapid testing: these tests were used for 46% of notified cases in 2025, up from 38% in 2024. Earlier diagnosis can mean earlier treatment, fewer opportunities for transmission and a better chance of preventing severe illness. It can also connect patients to appropriate treatment sooner, particularly when drug resistance is involved. Treatment needs support beyond medicine TB treatment usually lasts several months. Staying on medication can be difficult for people managing lost wages, food insecurity, travel costs, or stigma. A patient-centred response must address these barriers alongside the infection. The Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana provides nutritional support during TB treatment. Individuals and organisations can also register as Ni-kshay Mitras to offer patients additional assistance. These measures recognise that nutrition and practical support can influence a person’s ability to continue treatment and recover. From door-to-door screening to rapid testing, India is taking the fight against TB closer to communities. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) The government reported a 94% treatment success rate among people treated for drug-susceptible TB. This does not describe outcomes for every person with TB, including those with drug-resistant disease. For people facing long journeys or uncertain incomes, local follow-up can make the difference between starting and completing treatment. Linking health workers, families and community organisations helps keep patients connected to care. Counselling and follow-up can help patients navigate treatment. A TB patient support initiative illustrates why guidance matters alongside medicines. Accounts of people who have recovered from drug-resistant TB underline the importance of timely testing, appropriate treatment and sustained support. Turning progress into wider access The 38% decline measures a reduction in estimated deaths, not a fall in infections by the same proportion. Incidence counts new and recurrent cases arising in a population over time; mortality estimates deaths caused by the disease. WHO has not published a new incidence estimate for India in its 2026 report. The estimates are under review while district-level surveillance data collected in 2025 are analysed. Updated figures are expected in early 2027. The previous report estimated a 21% decline in incidence between 2015 and 2024, from 237 to 187 cases per lakh. This remains the latest comparable estimate, not a 2025 figure. The data gap makes stronger surveillance and reliable local information important. So is taking screening and diagnosis to remote and underserved communities. Rural health screening initiatives offer one way to bring early detection closer to people. TB specialists have also highlighted why treatment must be accompanied by attention to nutrition, living conditions and other health risks. India’s progress has come from combining different parts of the response: finding people earlier, improving access to rapid tests, supporting patients during treatment and strengthening community participation. The next step is to make these services dependable wherever a person lives, with prompt drug-resistance testing, uninterrupted medicines, nutritional support and follow-up. A fall in deaths means more people are surviving. Sustaining that progress will depend on ensuring fewer people are missed, and everyone diagnosed with TB can access and complete effective treatment. The 38% decline is a reason to build on what is working. items.title: What Happens to Your Old Clothes? Inside a Mumbai Network Turning 17500 Kg Into Income for Traders & Artisans
items.blurb: “Bhandiwala, bhandiwala.” For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas , he collected old clothes , traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused. He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them. But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little. That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi. Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas. “Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly,” he says. “We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages.” Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence. His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach. According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas , whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation. From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala . He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three. In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste. He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO. The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners? In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use. “Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved,” he tells The Better India . The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead. “At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system,” he says. People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils. Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai. They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. “I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends,” he recalls. “The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution.” TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. “We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it,” he explains. What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them? TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free. A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles. The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner. The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally. The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use. That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. “Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place,” Vikram says. “We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be.” Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners. Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route. TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders. It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation. Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use. Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre. For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations. TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected. ‘Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work’ TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households. TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work. Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers. “We had to go and search for clothes ourselves,” he says. “Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular.” For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar. He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat. Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes. “The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect,” he says. Now, he receives reusable garments from the team. “Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular,” he adds. He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine. Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations. Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping. “Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work,” he says. These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold. What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them. Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again? Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model. “The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it,” Vikram says. “There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system.” Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work. According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline. It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network. 17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next? The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests. Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month. The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them. For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place. There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested , the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply. The team can track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from. For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning. He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens. What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to. All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.blurb:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.
